title: Respiratory Terminology

sections.learningObjectives:
- Define common respiratory word parts, including roots, prefixes, and suffixes.
- Build and decode respiratory medical terms from their component word parts.
- Recognize common respiratory conditions by their terminology and key features.
- Identify common respiratory procedures and diagnostic tests by name and purpose.
- Apply scope-of-practice and safety principles when assisting with respiratory care, escalating concerns to the provider.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

A rhinoceros has a big horn on its nose — 'rhino' points to the nose, so rhin/o means nose.

### Question 2

When your nose runs like a faucet, that's rhinorrhea — 'rhino' (nose) plus 'rrhea' (flow).

### Question 3

Bronchitis is when the tubes that carry air inside your lungs get sore and swollen.

### Question 4

Laryngitis is when your voice box gets swollen, so your voice comes out scratchy or disappears.

### Question 5

Think 'pneumatic' — tools powered by air. Pneum/o is about air and the lungs that hold it.

### Question 6

When something ends in '-itis,' it's red, hot, and swollen — like a sore that got angry.

### Question 7

Trache/o sounds like 'trachea' — the tube (windpipe) air travels through.

### Question 8

A tracheostomy makes a new 'door' into the windpipe so air can get in when the usual path is blocked.

### Question 9

Thorac/o = chest — the area protected by your ribs, where your heart and lungs live.

### Question 10

'Hemo' = blood, and '-ptysis' = spitting. Hemoptysis is coughing up blood — always important to tell a provider.

### Question 11

Alveoli are the tiny balloons at the end of your lungs' tubes where oxygen hops into your blood.

### Question 12

Pharyng/o = your throat — the tunnel at the back of your mouth that food and air pass through.

### Question 13

Pneumonectomy = taking out a whole lung, like removing one whole balloon from a pair.

### Question 14

Thoracentesis is like carefully draining extra water out of the space around a balloon (lung) with a thin straw.

### Question 15

Bronchoscopy is sending a tiny camera down the windpipe to look at the air tubes inside the lungs.

### Question 16

Spirometry is a test where you blow into a machine to show how strong your lungs are.

### Question 17

Orthopnea means you breathe easier sitting straight up than lying flat — like needing pillows to sleep.

### Question 18

Pneumonia is when the tiny air balloons in your lungs get infected and fill with fluid, making it hard to breathe.

### Question 19

Asthma makes the air tubes in your lungs squeeze shut and get puffy, so air has a hard time getting through.

### Question 20

COPD means the airways are slowly and permanently blocked, making it hard to push air out.

### Question 21

Emphysema is when the tiny balloons in your lungs get holes and stretch out, so they can't push air out well.

### Question 22

Chronic bronchitis is when the air tubes stay irritated and make too much mucus, so you keep coughing.

### Question 23

Pneumothorax is a leak of air into the space around a lung, like a balloon deflating inside your chest.

### Question 24

Hemothorax is blood pooling in the space around the lungs inside your chest.

### Question 25

Pulmonary edema is like the lungs filling with water, making it hard to get air.

### Question 26

A pulmonary embolism is a clump that gets stuck in the lung's blood pipe, blocking blood flow.

### Question 27

Pleurisy is when the thin wrapper around your lungs gets irritated, so breathing hurts.

### Question 28

Atelectasis is when part of a lung goes flat like a deflated balloon instead of staying puffed up.

### Question 29

Epistaxis is the fancy doctor word for a nosebleed.

### Question 30

Sinusitis is when the little air pockets in your face get swollen and stuffed up.

### Question 31

Rhinitis is a runny, sneezy nose. Sinusitis is when the cheek and forehead areas hurt too.

### Question 32

Pharyngitis is a sore throat — the tunnel at the back of your mouth feeling scratchy and raw.

### Question 33

TB is a germ that usually sets up camp in the lungs and makes them sick.

### Question 34

Cystic fibrosis makes the body's mucus too thick and glue-like, clogging the lungs.

### Question 35

Sleep apnea is when a person's breathing stops and starts over and over while they sleep.

### Question 36

A pulse oximeter is a little clip on your finger that shines a light to see how much oxygen is in your blood.

### Question 37

A peak flow meter is a tube you blow into as hard as you can to see how open your airways are.

### Question 38

An incentive spirometer is like a game where you suck in air to lift a ball, which keeps your lungs puffed up.

### Question 39

A nebulizer turns liquid medicine into a cloud you breathe in.

### Question 40

A chest X-ray is a picture of the inside of your chest, like a photo that shows your lungs and heart.

### Question 41

An ABG is a blood test from an artery that checks the balance of oxygen and carbon dioxide in your blood.

### Question 42

Postural drainage is tilting the body so mucus can slide out of the lungs with the help of gravity.

### Question 43

A PFT is like a checkup for your lungs that measures how much and how fast you can breathe.

### Question 44

'Hyper' means a lot — hyperpnea is breathing faster and deeper than usual.

### Question 45

Hypoxia is when your body's cells aren't getting enough oxygen to do their jobs.

### Question 46

Laryngoscopy is using a tiny camera to look at your voice box.

### Question 47

Emphysema breaks the little balloons in the lungs, while chronic bronchitis makes the air tubes swollen and full of mucus.

### Question 48

Asthma is like a door that gets stuck but can be opened again, while COPD is a door that slowly stays shut.

### Question 49

COPD is a big umbrella covering two lung problems: the swollen-tube kind (bronchitis) and the broken-balloon kind (emphysema).

### Question 50

Hypoxemia is low oxygen in the 'river' (blood); hypoxia is low oxygen reaching the 'fields' (your cells).

### Question 51

If someone suddenly has chest pain and can't breathe well, you tell the doctor right away — like pulling a fire alarm.

### Question 52

If the oxygen number is way too low, that's like a low battery warning — you tell an adult (the provider) right away.

### Question 53

The assistant is like the helper who shows the teacher the test; the teacher (provider) is the one who explains the score.

### Question 54

Oxygen is medicine, so only the doctor can say when and how much to use — like needing a prescription.

### Question 55

Coughing up blood is a big warning sign — you always tell the doctor, never just wait and see.

### Question 56

For a nosebleed, sit up and lean a little forward so blood drips out, not down your throat — and let the doctor know.

### Question 57

If someone suddenly can't breathe and their chest hurts, get the doctor right away — don't make them wait.

### Question 58

Blue lips are like a car's overheating light — a warning that the body may not be getting enough oxygen.

### Question 59

TB travels through the air, so you wear the right mask and follow the office rules to keep everyone safe.

### Question 60

Tracheotomy is making the cut; tracheostomy is the little door (opening) left behind.

### Question 61

The assistant helps with positioning, but the doctor or therapist calls the shots on the chest therapy — like a helper, not the coach.

### Question 62

The assistant reads the number and shows it to the doctor; the doctor explains what it means.

### Question 63

The assistant cheers the patient on and writes down the numbers; the doctor reads the results.

### Question 64

If the 'blow test' numbers keep going down, it's like a warning light — tell the doctor so they can help before it gets worse.
